title: Six Degrees of Exposure
primary_metric: modeled transmission-weight (summed contact-event edge weight) eliminated per dose spent, where 'per dose spent' means per the shared, fixed dose-and-outreach budget both operations draw down identically

options.A: Operation Hub Sweep — vaccinate the 50 highest-degree individuals identified from the traced contact network
options.B: Operation Wide Net — vaccinate 500 individuals chosen at random from the same traced population, same total dose budget

sources.title: Panzarasa P, Opsahl T, Carley KM. "Patterns and dynamics of users' behavior and interaction: Network analysis of an online community." J Am Soc Inf Sci Technol 60(5):911-932 (2009). Distributed as the "CollegeMsg temporal network."
sources.note: Raw edge list fetched directly from https://snap.stanford.edu/data/CollegeMsg.txt.gz (345,339 bytes, 59,835 rows of 'source target unix-timestamp'). This case aggregated it into an undirected simple weighted graph: each unordered pair with >=1 interaction becomes one edge, weighted by its total interaction count. That produced 13,838 edges -- different from SNAP's own posted 'edges in static graph: 20,296' figure, which counts the *directed* static graph instead. Degree statistics, the top-50 ranked list (Appendix B), and the sample subgraph (Appendix C) are this case's own computation over the aggregated graph, not figures printed on the source's page. Used as a structural stand-in for a real county contact-tracing network -- see Appendix E, MA1.

deliverables.text: A labeled, weighted diagram of the sample contact subgraph (Appendix C): every vertex drawn and labeled with its traced ID, every edge drawn and labeled with its weight.
A ranked degree table (Appendix B): the 50 individuals with the highest degree in the full traced network.

A transmission-weight-eliminated comparison table (Appendices A, B) for Operation Hub Sweep vs Operation Wide Net -- Wide Net via the counting argument, Hub Sweep via Appendix B's weighted-degree sum minus its disclosed internal-edge double-count correction -- plus a budget-consistency check against Appendix D.
A shortest notification-path calculation (Appendix C) comparing at least two candidate paths by total notification cost.

balance.argument_a: The 50 highest-degree individuals (Appendix B) touch 5,859 distinct edges carrying a combined weight of 27,643 -- 46.2% of the network's total 59,835 contact-weight, from just 2.6% of the traced population.
balance.argument_b: Hub identification depends on contact-tracing fieldwork that is slower and costlier (Appendix D: $213.94/dose vs $38.00/dose), which is exactly why Hub Sweep buys only 50 doses against Wide Net's 500 for a comparable spend, and Wide Net's 500 doses are spread across the whole traced population rather than a fixed, already-identified list -- giving it a structural chance at an emerging cluster Hub Sweep's list cannot reach.
balance.margin_basis: Compare total edge-weight eliminated for Hub Sweep's fixed 50-person set (27,643, exact) against the expected total edge-weight eliminated for Wide Net's random 500-person set (59,835 x [1-(1399x1398)/(1899x1898)] = 27,366.7, found via a counting/expected-value argument since a random selection cannot be enumerated by hand). Both are drawn from the same sourced 59,835-weight network (Appendix A, S3).

cohort_bands.note: Split the room into two operations desks -- one builds D2/D3 for Hub Sweep, one for Wide Net -- and have them trade tables before the Data Deep Dive comparison.
Work one shared D3 table on the board together rather than splitting into desks; keep D4's shortest-path exercise as paired work.

No vote at Anchor 1 -- the learner states an initial position, and the guide argues the other side directly. Spend the recovered time on D3's counting argument for Wide Net's expected value, the least intuitive step to do alone.

modeling_assumptions.value_used: Modeled using the real, public CollegeMsg dataset (Panzarasa, Opsahl & Carley, 2009; distributed by Stanford SNAP) as a structural stand-in for Calloway County's actual contact-tracing graph
modeling_assumptions.basis: Real public-health contact-tracing data is protected health information and cannot be published for a classroom exercise. CollegeMsg is a real, public, anonymized person-to-person interaction network of a comparable, classroom-workable size (1,899 people) with the same qualitative shape -- a small number of highly-connected people and a long tail of lightly-connected ones -- that the network-epidemiology literature uses for exactly this targeted-vs-random comparison.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The case's entire primary-metric margin (Appendix A/B data) depends on this specific network's actual degree distribution. A different real network with a different skew could change the margin or flip which operation wins -- that dependency is the honest core of the case, not a flaw to be hidden.

modeling_assumptions.value_used: Each edge's weight is treated as its number of recorded contact events, standing in for how often two traced individuals were in contact during the surveillance window
modeling_assumptions.basis: The source dataset's edges are private-message counts between two people; this case treats repeated messages as a proxy for repeated real-world contact, the same substitution MA1 already makes at the network level.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Does not change which edges exist, only how heavier edges are interpreted; does not affect the primary-metric arithmetic, which only needs the weight values themselves.

modeling_assumptions.value_used: Fixed at 50 (Hub Sweep) and 500 (Wide Net), as stated in the case brief
modeling_assumptions.basis: Calloway County is fictional; its real budget and internal per-dose costs are not public record. Appendix D's real, sourced national-median costs do not, at their exact values, divide one shared budget into precisely 50 and 500 -- the case fixes the headcounts directly rather than forcing a fit to national data that would not represent one specific county's real contract rates anyway.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Does not affect the primary-metric comparison in D3's first half (which uses Appendix A/B network data directly, independent of Appendix D). It is the reason D3's second half exists -- to make the discrepancy (50 stated vs ~88.8 implied by national medians) a Hero must reckon with, rather than a fact hidden in a footnote.

sensitivity_note: This case models a real disease outbreak and a real vaccination-response decision. Framing is deliberately protection-oriented throughout (doses delivered, contacts reached, connections removed from further spread) and never asks students to compute or optimize a casualty count, consistent with SPEC §6. The facilitator should still flag, before discussion, that some learners may have personal experience with contact tracing, quarantine, or vaccination-access decisions (COVID-19 and other outbreaks) and that this can surface real feelings even in a protection-framed case -- give it room rather than rushing into the arithmetic.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: Calloway County is fictional and its real budget/staffing split between the two operations is not public record (Appendix D, MA3), so n_wide=500 is fixed as the county's stated operational plan rather than derived from a source; sensitivity_model.py shows a +/-50% sweep of n_wide both breaks the 20% balance cap and, at +50%, flips the winner from A to B, so this assumption is genuinely load-bearing and is disclosed here rather than eliminated.
